courses.title: Trigonometry
courses.summary: From right-triangle ratios to the unit circle, identities, and the calculus that harmonises them. Built for learners who have never met sine before.

layers.title: Geometric Ratios & Right Triangles
objectives: Name the three sides of a right triangle relative to a chosen angle
Compute sine, cosine, and tangent as pure side ratios
Use SOH-CAH-TOA without memorising numbers
Recognise why the ratios do not depend on triangle size

concepts.definition: The ratio of the side opposite angle θ to the hypotenuse in a right triangle: sin θ = opposite / hypotenuse.
The ratio of the side adjacent to angle θ (the leg touching it, not the hypotenuse) to the hypotenuse: cos θ = adjacent / hypotenuse.
The ratio of the opposite leg to the adjacent leg: tan θ = opposite / adjacent, equivalently sin θ / cos θ.
The longest side of a right triangle, opposite the 90° angle. It is the denominator of both sine and cosine.

layers.intuition: Scale a right triangle up or down and the *angles* stay the same while the sides change. That means any ratio of two sides is a fingerprint of the angle alone. Charts of sine values are really charts of triangle shapes — that is why one table works for every size of triangle.

worked.problem: In a right triangle the side opposite θ is 3, the adjacent side is 4, and the hypotenuse is 5. Find sin θ, cos θ, and tan θ.
steps: Identify the hypotenuse: the side across from the right angle, length 5.
sin θ = opposite / hypotenuse = 3 / 5 = 0.6.
cos θ = adjacent / hypotenuse = 4 / 5 = 0.8.
tan θ = opposite / adjacent = 3 / 4 = 0.75. Check: sin / cos = 0.6 / 0.8 = 0.75 ✓
worked.answer: sin θ = 0.6, cos θ = 0.8, tan θ = 0.75

Computing a ratio upside down; sin is always opposite over hypotenuse, never hypotenuse over opposite.

scenario.q: A ramp rises 1 m over a horizontal run of 4 m. Which ratio directly gives the ramp angle?
scenario.why: The rise (1 m) is opposite the incline angle and the run (4 m) is adjacent, so tan θ = rise / run = 1 / 4, giving θ ≈ 14°.

layers.title: The Unit Circle & Radians
objectives: Convert between degrees and radians exactly
Read sine and cosine as coordinates on the unit circle
Locate angles in all four quadrants using reference angles
Derive arc length and sector area from radians

concepts.definition: The angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc equal in length to the radius. A full turn is 2π radians = 360°, so 1 radian ≈ 57.3°.
The circle of radius 1 centred at the origin. A point at angle θ has coordinates (cos θ, sin θ), which extends trigonometry beyond 0°–90°.
The acute angle between the terminal side of θ and the nearest x-axis; it supplies the magnitude of sin and cos while the quadrant supplies the sign.
For a circle of radius r and central angle θ in radians, arc length s = rθ. Using degrees instead would require the extra factor π/180.

layers.intuition: A right triangle only describes angles up to 90°. Rotate the hypotenuse around the origin at fixed length 1 and its tip sweeps the unit circle: the x-coordinate is cos θ, the y-coordinate is sin θ. Now every angle, including negative and >360° ones, has a coordinate pair, and the signs come from the quadrant rather than from a triangle.

worked.problem: Convert 135° to radians and evaluate sin 135° and cos 135°.
steps: Multiply by π/180: 135 · π/180 = 3π/4.
The reference angle is 180° − 135° = 45°, so magnitudes are sin 45° = √2/2 and cos 45° = √2/2.
135° sits in quadrant II: x < 0, y > 0.
Therefore cos 135° = −√2/2 and sin 135° = +√2/2.

scenario.why: s = rθ = 0.4 · 3 = 1.2 m. Multiplying by π/180 here would be a unit error.

layers.title: Graphs & Periodicity
objectives: Identify amplitude, period, phase shift, and vertical shift from a formula
Sketch sine, cosine, and tangent families
Model a repeating real-world signal
Explain why tangent has asymptotes

concepts.definition: Half the distance between a periodic function's maximum and minimum. For y = A sin(Bx + C) + D the amplitude is |A|.
The horizontal length of one full cycle. For sine and cosine the period is 2π/|B|; for tangent it is π/|B|.
The horizontal translation of a wave, equal to −C/B in y = A sin(Bx + C) + D. Positive C shifts the graph left.
A vertical line the graph approaches but never touches. tan x has asymptotes at x = π/2 + kπ because cosine is zero there.

layers.intuition: Read a transformed wave as a recipe, not a formula: A stretches it vertically, B compresses it horizontally, C slides it sideways, D lifts the centreline. Because sine and cosine are the same wave offset by a quarter turn, every cosine graph is a shifted sine — choosing which to use is a modelling convenience, not a mathematical difference.

worked.problem: Describe and sketch one period of y = 3 sin(2x − π/2) + 1.
steps: Amplitude |A| = 3, so the wave oscillates between 1 − 3 = −2 and 1 + 3 = 4.
The midline is y = 1 (the vertical shift D).
Period = 2π / |B| = 2π/2 = π.
Phase shift = −C/B = −(−π/2)/2 = π/4 to the right.
Plot key points π/4 apart: start at midline rising, then max 4, midline 1, min −2, midline 1.
worked.answer: Amplitude 3, period π, shift π/4 right, midline y = 1, range [−2, 4]

scenario.q: A tide has a high of 5 m at 02:00 and a low of 1 m at 08:00. Which model fits?
scenario.why: Amplitude = (5 − 1)/2 = 2, midline = 3, half-cycle (high to low) is 6 h so the period is 12 h giving B = 2π/12 = π/6, and a cosine peaks at t = 2.

layers.title: Identities & Equations
objectives: Prove the Pythagorean identity from the unit circle
Simplify expressions with sum, difference, and double-angle identities
Solve trigonometric equations on a given interval
Use identities to avoid dividing by zero

concepts.definition: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 for every θ. It follows directly from the unit circle equation x² + y² = 1.
sin(A ± B) = sin A cos B ± cos A sin B, and cos(A ± B) = cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B. These generate every other identity.
sin 2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ and cos 2θ = cos²θ − sin²θ = 1 − 2sin²θ = 2cos²θ − 1.
Because sine and cosine repeat every 2π, an equation such as sin θ = 0.5 has solutions θ = π/6 + 2kπ and θ = 5π/6 + 2kπ for integer k.

layers.intuition: Identities are not a list to memorise; they are one fact — the unit circle — rewritten. Anything you can prove from sin² + cos² = 1, you own forever. When solving an equation, isolate one trigonometric function, find the principal solutions in one cycle, then add the period to capture the rest. Dividing both sides by cos θ is the classic way to lose solutions.

worked.problem: Solve 2sin²θ − sin θ − 1 = 0 for 0 ≤ θ < 2π.
steps: Treat sin θ as a single variable u: 2u² − u − 1 = 0.
Factor: (2u + 1)(u − 1) = 0, so u = −1/2 or u = 1.
sin θ = 1 gives θ = π/2.
sin θ = −1/2 gives reference angle π/6 in quadrants III and IV: θ = 7π/6 and θ = 11π/6.
Collect all solutions in the interval.

Forgetting the second solution a reference angle produces in another quadrant.
Applying a double-angle identity to sin(2θ) when the argument is really 2 sin θ.

scenario.q: You simplify sin θ · cos θ. Which single expression is equivalent?
scenario.why: The double-angle identity rear-ranged: ½ sin 2θ = ½ · 2 sin θ cos θ = sin θ cos θ.

layers.title: Advanced Applications & Calculus Integration
objectives: Differentiate and integrate sine and cosine from the unit circle
Model harmonic motion with amplitude-phase form
Use inverse trigonometry in real geometry problems
Recognise where Fourier analysis extends the same wave idea

concepts.definition: d/dx sin x = cos x and d/dx cos x = −sin x (x in radians). The radian requirement exists because the limit sin h / h → 1 only holds in radians.
A quantity oscillating about equilibrium is written x(t) = A cos(ωt + φ), where ω is angular frequency and φ the phase; period T = 2π/ω.
arcsin y returns the angle in [−π/2, π/2] whose sine is y. The restriction guarantees a single-valued inverse.
Any reasonably well-behaved periodic signal can be written as a sum of sines and cosines at integer multiples of its base frequency; coefficients come from integrating the signal against those waves.

layers.intuition: Sine and cosine are each other's derivative up to a sign, which is exactly the signature of circular motion: velocity is perpendicular to position. That single geometric fact powers simple harmonic motion, AC circuits, signal processing, and the Fourier transform — all of them are statement that a wave can be differentiated, added, and decomposed without ever leaving the family.

worked.problem: A mass on a spring has position x(t) = 0.08 cos(6t) metres. Find its maximum speed and the first time it passes equilibrium.
steps: Velocity is the derivative: v(t) = −0.08 · 6 sin(6t) = −0.48 sin(6t).
Maximum speed is the amplitude of velocity: |−0.48| = 0.48 m/s.
Equilibrium means x = 0, so cos(6t) = 0.
First positive solution: 6t = π/2, so t = π/12 ≈ 0.262 s.
At that moment sin(6t) = 1, confirming maximum speed at the crossing.
worked.answer: v_max = 0.48 m/s; first equilibrium crossing at t = π/12 s

layers.diagram:
flowchart LR
  S[sin x] -->|d/dx| C[cos x]
  C -->|d/dx| NS["−sin x"]
  NS -->|d/dx| NC["−cos x"]
  NC -->|d/dx| S
  S --> H[Harmonic motion]
  H --> F[Fourier decomposition]
pitfalls: Differentiating in degrees, which introduces a stray factor of π/180.
Forgetting that integrating sine yields a negative cosine.
Using arcsin outside [−1, 1] and expecting a real angle.

scenario.q: What is ∫₀^π sin x dx?
scenario.why: The antiderivative is −cos x, evaluated: (−cos π) − (−cos 0) = 1 + 1 = 2, the area of one positive arch.

courses.title: Calculus
courses.summary: Limits, derivatives, integrals, and the machinery of change — rebuilt from first principles so nothing is a rule without a reason.

layers.title: Limits & Continuity
objectives: Read limit notation as a prediction, not an evaluation
Compute limits by substitution, factoring, and rationalising
Distinguish removable, jump, and infinite discontinuities
Explain why 0/0 is indeterminate rather than undefined

concepts.definition: lim(x→a) f(x) = L means f(x) can be made arbitrarily close to L by taking x sufficiently close to a, without requiring f(a) to equal L.
The value approached from one side only: x→a⁺ (larger values) or x→a⁻. A two-sided limit exists exactly when both one-sided limits exist and agree.
f is continuous at a when f(a) is defined, lim(x→a) f(x) exists, and the two are equal. All three conditions must hold.
An expression such as 0/0 or ∞/∞ that does not by itself determine a value; the limit must be resolved through algebra or L'Hôpital's rule.

layers.intuition: A limit asks "where is the function heading?", not "where does it land?". This distinction is the entire foundation of calculus: the derivative is a limit of slopes at a point the two sample points never actually reach. Continuity is the extra promise that the landing spot equals the destination.

worked.problem: Evaluate lim(x→2) (x² − 4)/(x − 2).
steps: Direct substitution gives 0/0 — indeterminate, so factor instead of concluding "undefined".
Factor the numerator: (x − 2)(x + 2).
Cancel the common factor for x ≠ 2: the expression becomes x + 2.
Now substitute: 2 + 2 = 4.
The original function has a removable hole at x = 2, but the limit is still 4.

scenario.q: What is lim(x→0) sin x / x?
scenario.why: Substitution gives 0/0, but the small-angle geometry of the unit circle bounds cos x ≤ sin x / x ≤ 1, so the squeeze theorem forces the limit to 1.

layers.title: Derivatives from First Principles
objectives: Build the derivative as a limit of secant slopes
Differentiate polynomials, products, quotients, and compositions
Interpret the derivative as instantaneous rate and tangent slope
Explain why differentiability implies continuity but not the converse

concepts.definition: The average rate of change over an interval: [f(x + h) − f(x)] / h. Its limit as h→0 is the derivative.
f′(x) = lim(h→0) [f(x + h) − f(x)] / h — the instantaneous rate of change, equal to the slope of the tangent line at x.
For a composition, d/dx f(g(x)) = f′(g(x)) · g′(x). Differentiate the outside, then multiply by the inside's derivative.
f is differentiable at a when the derivative limit exists. This requires continuity at a, but continuity does not imply differentiability (|x| at 0 is the standard counterexample).

layers.intuition: Slope needs two points; instantaneous change needs one. The difference quotient bridges them, and the limit performs the leap. Practically, f′(a) answers "if I nudge the input by a tiny amount, how much does the output move?" — that reading survives into gradients, sensitivity analysis, and physics.

worked.problem: Differentiate f(x) = (3x² + 1)⁵.
steps: Identify the composition: outer u⁵, inner u = 3x² + 1.
Differentiate the outer with respect to u: 5u⁴.
Differentiate the inner: d/dx (3x² + 1) = 6x.
Multiply (chain rule): f′(x) = 5(3x² + 1)⁴ · 6x.
Simplify: f′(x) = 30x(3x² + 1)⁴.

scenario.q: A balloon's radius grows at 2 cm/s. How fast is its volume growing when r = 5 cm? (V = 4/3 πr³)
scenario.why: dV/dt = 4πr² · dr/dt = 4π(25)(2) = 200π cm³/s.

layers.title: Applications of Derivatives
objectives: Find critical points and classify them with derivative tests
Solve constrained optimisation problems
Use the mean value theorem as a guarantee
Interpret second derivatives as concavity and acceleration

concepts.definition: A point in the domain where f′(x) = 0 or f′ does not exist. Local extrema can only occur at critical points or endpoints.
If f′ changes from positive to negative across a critical point, it is a local maximum; negative to positive gives a local minimum; no sign change gives neither.
f is concave up where f″ > 0 (tangent lines below the curve) and concave down where f″ < 0. An inflection point is where concavity changes.
In optimisation, the relation among variables (e.g. perimeter = 40) used to express the objective in one variable before differentiating.

layers.intuition: Derivatives turn shape questions into algebra. "Where is the biggest?" becomes "where is the slope zero and switching sign?" The second derivative tells you how the rate itself is changing, which is why it distinguishes a peak from a valley and acceleration from velocity. Always check endpoints: a closed interval can hide its extreme value at the boundary.

worked.problem: A rectangle has perimeter 40 m. What dimensions maximise its area?
steps: Let width = x and height = y, with 2x + 2y = 40 so y = 20 − x.
Objective: A(x) = x(20 − x) = 20x − x².
Differentiate: A′(x) = 20 − 2x.
Set A′ = 0: x = 10. Since A″ = −2 < 0, this is a maximum.
Then y = 20 − 10 = 10, so the maximum area is a square of 100 m².
worked.answer: A 10 m × 10 m square, area 100 m²

options: f′ does not change sign there; it is an inflection point

scenario.why: f′ = 3x² is non-negative on both sides, so the function keeps increasing through the flat spot. f″ = 0 confirms an inflection, not an extremum.

layers.title: Integration & the Fundamental Theorem
objectives: Approximate area with Riemann sums and pass to the definite integral
Use the fundamental theorem to evaluate integrals exactly
Integrate by substitution and by parts
Interpret signed area and net change

concepts.definition: An approximation of area under a curve by summing rectangles: Σ f(xᵢ) Δx. The definite integral is the limit as the partition becomes infinitely fine.
∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx is the signed area between f and the x-axis from a to b — area below the axis counts as negative.
If F is an antiderivative of f, then ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a). It links accumulation (integrals) with rates (derivatives) as inverse operations.
The chain rule run backwards: replace u = g(x), du = g′(x) dx, turning a composite integrand into a simpler one.

layers.intuition: Integration is accumulation. Slice a quantity into thin pieces, add the pieces, and take the limit — that recipe computes area, distance from velocity, mass from density, and probability from a density curve. The fundamental theorem is the punchline: accumulating a rate recovers the original quantity, which is why integrals and derivatives undo each other.

worked.problem: Evaluate ∫₁⁴ (2x + 1) dx.
steps: Find an antiderivative: F(x) = x² + x.
Apply the fundamental theorem: F(4) − F(1).
Subtract: 20 − 2 = 18.

scenario.q: A particle has velocity v(t) = 3t² m/s. How far does it travel from t = 0 to t = 2 s?
scenario.why: Distance = ∫₀² 3t² dt = [t³]₀² = 8 − 0 = 8 m.

layers.title: Series, Multivariable & Differential Equations
objectives: Expand a function as a Taylor series and bound the error
Compute partial derivatives and interpret the gradient
Solve separable first-order differential equations
Recognise when a series converges absolutely

concepts.definition: f(x) = Σ f⁽ⁿ⁾(a)(x − a)ⁿ / n! near x = a. Truncating after n terms leaves an error governed by the next term.
∂f/∂x measures how f changes as x varies while every other input is held fixed. It is an ordinary derivative in a slice of the domain.
The vector of all partial derivatives, ∇f. It points in the direction of steepest ascent and is orthogonal to level curves — the basis of gradient descent.
A differential equation writable as dy/dx = g(x)h(y). Rearranging to dy/h(y) = g(x) dx and integrating both sides solves it.

layers.intuition: Locally, every smooth function is a polynomial — that is the Taylor promise, and it is how calculators, physics engines, and neural network initialisations actually compute sine and exp. In several variables the derivative stops being a number and becomes a direction: the gradient tells you which way is uphill, which is precisely the information optimisation algorithms need.

worked.problem: Solve dy/dx = 2xy with y(0) = 3.
steps: Separate: dy/y = 2x dx (valid where y ≠ 0).
Integrate both sides: ln|y| = x² + C.
Exponentiate: y = A e^{x²}.
Apply the initial condition: 3 = A e⁰ = A.
Write the particular solution and note it is valid for all real x.
worked.answer: y = 3e^{x²}

courses.title: Linear Algebra
courses.summary: Vectors, matrices, and the geometry of transformations — the language underneath graphics, machine learning, and quantum mechanics.

layers.title: Vectors & Geometric Intuition
objectives: Add and scale vectors geometrically and algebraically
Compute dot products and interpret them as projection
Distinguish span from a single vector
Measure length with the Euclidean norm

concepts.definition: An ordered list of numbers representing a magnitude and direction in space; in n dimensions it is an element of ℝⁿ.
A sum c₁v₁ + c₂v₂ + … + cₙvₙ with scalar weights cᵢ. Nearly every idea in linear algebra is a statement about which combinations are possible.
The set of all linear combinations of a collection of vectors — the reachable subspace. Two non-parallel vectors in ℝ² span the whole plane.
u · v = Σ uᵢvᵢ = |u||v| cos θ. Zero means orthogonal; the sign reveals whether vectors point broadly together or apart.

layers.intuition: A vector is not an arrow in a picture; it is a recipe of coordinates. Addition is "do both displacements", scaling is "do it more or less". The dot product converts geometry into arithmetic: it measures how much of one vector lies along another, which is how projection, correlation, and attention scores all work.

worked.problem: For u = (3, −1) and v = (2, 4), compute u + v, 2u − v, and u · v.
steps: Add componentwise: u + v = (3 + 2, −1 + 4) = (5, 3).
Scale then subtract: 2u = (6, −2), so 2u − v = (6 − 2, −2 − 4) = (4, −6).
Since the dot product is non-zero, the vectors are not orthogonal.

scenario.q: u = (1, 2) and v = (2, 4). What is their span?
options: A plane not through the origin
scenario.why: v = 2u, so the two vectors are parallel and every combination lands on the same line through the origin.

layers.title: Matrices as Transformations
objectives: Multiply a matrix by a vector as a combination of columns
Recognise identity, rotation, scaling, and shear matrices
Compute determinants and interpret them as area scaling
Invert a 2×2 matrix and know when it fails

concepts.definition: A rectangular array of numbers acting on vectors by linear transformation; an m×n matrix maps ℝⁿ to ℝᵐ.
det[[a, b], [c, d]] = ad − bc. Its absolute value is the area scale factor of the transformation; zero means the map collapses space and is not invertible.
A⁻¹ satisfies A⁻¹A = AA⁻¹ = I. For 2×2, A⁻¹ = (1/det A)[[d, −b], [−c, a]], and it exists only when det A ≠ 0.
A map T with T(u + v) = T(u) + T(v) and T(cu) = cT(u). Every such map is multiplication by some matrix.

layers.intuition: A matrix is not a table of data — it is a machine that moves space. Columns tell you where the basis vectors land, and everything else follows by linearity. The determinant is the machine's volume dial: 2 doubles areas, 0 flattens the plane into a line, and a negative value means orientation was flipped.

worked.problem: Let A = [[2, 1], [1, 3]] and v = (1, 2). Compute Av and det A.
steps: Treat the columns: col₁ = (2, 1), col₂ = (1, 3).
A non-zero determinant means A is invertible and scales area by 5.
worked.answer: Av = (4, 7), det A = 5

  D --> Z{det = 0?}
  Z -->|Yes| C[Collapses space: no inverse]
  Z -->|No| I[Invertible: A⁻¹ exists]
pitfalls: Multiplying matrices in the wrong order — AB ≠ BA in general.
Assuming a matrix is invertible just because it is square.
Reading determinant as a slope rather than a signed area scale.

scenario.q: A = [[1, 2], [2, 4]]. What happens to the plane under A?
options: It collapses onto a line because det A = 0
scenario.why: det A = 1·4 − 2·2 = 0, so the columns are dependent and the image is one-dimensional.

layers.title: Systems of Equations & Elimination
objectives: Translate a linear system into an augmented matrix
Reduce to row echelon form with legal row operations
Classify systems as unique, infinite, or inconsistent via rank
Read free variables as degrees of freedom

concepts.definition: The coefficient matrix with the constant column appended. Row operations on it correspond exactly to legal equation manipulations.
A staircase pattern where each leading entry is right of the one above and rows of zeros sit at the bottom. Reached by Gaussian elimination.
The number of linearly independent rows (equivalently, pivots). It measures how much genuine information the system carries.
A variable without a pivot column; it can be chosen freely, and each one adds a parameter to the solution set.

layers.intuition: Elimination is disciplined substitution: use one equation to kill a variable in the others, then repeat on the smaller system. Rank is the audit that tells you what survived — equal rows mean redundancy, a pivot in the constant column means contradiction. "Infinite solutions" is not a failure; it is a description of a line or plane of answers.

worked.problem: Solve x + y + z = 6, 2x − y + z = 3, x + 2y − z = 2.
steps: Write the augmented matrix: [1 1 1 | 6; 2 −1 1 | 3; 1 2 −1 | 2].
From R₃: y − 2z = −4, so y = 2z − 4.
Then y = 2(3) − 4 = 2 and x = 6 − y − z = 1.

layers.diagram:
flowchart TD
  S[Linear system] --> A[Augmented matrix]
  A --> E[Gaussian elimination]
  E --> R[Row echelon form]
  R --> C{Contradiction row?}
  C -->|Yes| N[No solution]
  C -->|No| P{Pivot in every column?}
  P -->|Yes| U[Unique solution]
  P -->|No| I[Infinite family with parameters]
pitfalls: Scaling a row by zero — that destroys information and is not a legal operation.
Stopping at echelon form and forgetting back-substitution.
Confusing "more equations than unknowns" with "unique solution".

scenario.q: A 3×3 system reduces to rows [1 0 2 | 4], [0 1 −1 | 1], [0 0 0 | 0]. What is the solution set?
options: A line with one free variable
scenario.why: There are two pivots and no contradiction, so one variable (z) is free and the solution set is a line.

layers.title: Vector Spaces & Eigenvalues
objectives: Test whether a set of vectors forms a basis
Compute null space and column space dimensions
Find eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a small matrix
Explain diagonalisation and when it is possible

concepts.definition: A set of vectors that both spans the space and is linearly independent; every vector has exactly one coordinate representation in that basis.
The set of vectors x with Ax = 0. Its dimension is the number of free variables and measures how much information A destroys.
A non-zero vector v with Av = λv for some scalar λ. The transformation only stretches or flips it, never rotates it off its line.
Writing A = PDP⁻¹ where D is diagonal of eigenvalues and P holds eigenvectors. It is possible when there are enough independent eigenvectors.

layers.intuition: A basis is a coordinate system you choose, not one you are given. Changing basis can turn a tangled matrix into a diagonal one — the same transformation seen from its natural axes. Eigenvectors are those natural axes: directions the map respects. This is why page rank, vibration modes, and PCA all reduce to eigenproblems.

worked.problem: Find the eigenvalues of A = [[4, 1], [2, 3]].
steps: Solve det(A − λI) = 0.
Determinant: (4 − λ)(3 − λ) − 2 = λ² − 7λ + 12 − 2 = λ² − 7λ + 10.
Factor: (λ − 5)(λ − 2) = 0.
Eigenvalues are λ = 5 and λ = 2; both real, so A is diagonalisable over ℝ.
worked.answer: λ = 5 and λ = 2

  A[Matrix A] --> C[Column space]
  A --> N[Null space]
  C --> R[Rank r]
  N --> F[n − r free directions]
  A --> E[Eigen equation Av = λv]

pitfalls: Including the zero vector as an eigenvector — it satisfies the equation but is excluded by definition.
Assuming every matrix is diagonalisable.
Confusing the dimension of the column space with the number of columns.

scenario.q: A 4×4 matrix has rank 3. What is the dimension of its null space?
scenario.why: Rank-nullity: nullity = n − rank = 4 − 3 = 1.

layers.title: Orthogonality, SVD & Applications
objectives: Project a vector onto a subspace and derive least squares
Orthogonalise a basis with Gram–Schmidt
Interpret the singular value decomposition geometrically
Connect SVD to compression and principal components

concepts.definition: The closest point in a subspace to a given vector: proj_u v = (v · u / u · u) u for a line spanned by u.
When Ax = b has no exact solution, minimise ‖Ax − b‖². The optimum solves the normal equations AᵀAx = Aᵀb.
A procedure converting any independent set into an orthonormal basis by subtracting projections onto the vectors already built.
A = UΣVᵀ for any matrix: rotate by Vᵀ, scale by Σ, rotate by U. Singular values are the stretch factors along principal axes.

layers.intuition: Orthogonality is the geometry of "no interference": components can be analysed one at a time. Projection is the best approximation in a subspace, which is exactly what least-squares regression does. SVD generalises eigenvectors to non-square matrices and ranks the directions of a dataset by importance — truncate the small singular values and you get compression and PCA.

worked.problem: Project v = (3, 4) onto the line spanned by u = (1, 0), then onto u = (1, 1).
steps: Onto (1, 0): (v · u)/(u · u) = 3, so the projection is (3, 0).
Onto (1, 1): v · u = 3 + 4 = 7 and u · u = 2, so the coefficient is 3.5.
The projection is 3.5(1, 1) = (3.5, 3.5).
The residual (3, 4) − (3.5, 3.5) = (−0.5, 0.5) is orthogonal to (1, 1), confirming minimal distance.
worked.answer: (3, 0) onto the x-axis; (3.5, 3.5) onto y = x

Best for
rows: Solving many systems with one matrix

layers.diagram:
flowchart LR
  B[b vector] --> P[Project onto column space]
  P --> R[Residual orthogonal]
  R --> N[Normal equations AᵀAx = Aᵀb]
  A[Matrix A] --> S[SVD A = UΣVᵀ]

pitfalls: Projecting onto a vector without dividing by u · u.
Forgetting to re-orthogonalise against all previous vectors in Gram–Schmidt.
Assuming singular values can be negative — they are non-negative by construction.

scenario.q: A 1000×1000 image matrix has only 20 significant singular values. What does that imply?
options: It can be stored approximately with ~40,000 numbers instead of 1,000,000
scenario.why: Rank-20 truncation stores 1000·20 (U) + 20 (Σ) + 20·1000 (Vᵀ) ≈ 40,020 values while preserving the dominant structure.

courses.title: Data Structures
courses.summary: Arrays to union-find — how memory layout and invariants decide whether your program is instant or unusable at scale.

layers.title: Arrays, Strings & Complexity
objectives: Explain contiguous memory and constant-time indexing
Measure operations with big-O on realistic inputs
Distinguish worst case, average case, and amortised cost
Choose between a static array and a dynamic array

concepts.definition: A contiguous block of equal-sized elements addressed by index. Because the address is base + index × size, access is O(1).
An upper bound on growth: f(n) = O(g(n)) means f grows no faster than a constant multiple of g for large n. It describes scaling, not seconds.
The average cost per operation across a sequence. Dynamic array appends are O(1) amortised because resizing doubles capacity and happens geometrically rarely.
The performance benefit of accessing memory that is already in CPU cache. Sequential array scans beat pointer-chasing structures even at equal big-O.

layers.intuition: An array is fast because it is boring: fixed stride, no indirection, perfect for the prefetcher. Complexity analysis explains the wall you hit at scale, but constants and cache behaviour decide close races. Insert at the front of an array and every later element must shift — that O(n) is the price of contiguity.

worked.problem: A dynamic array holds 8 elements and doubles when full. How many total element copies occur across 16 appends starting from empty?
steps: Resizes happen at capacities 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 while growing to 17 elements.
Copy counts: 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 31.
Total work for 17 appends is 31 copies plus 17 writes.
Copies per append ≈ 31/17 < 2, a constant — hence O(1) amortised.
worked.answer: 31 copies for 17 appends: constant amortised overhead

layers.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Append] --> F{Capacity full?}
  F -->|No| W[Write at length, O(1)]
  F -->|Yes| D[Allocate 2× capacity]
  D --> C[Copy n elements, O(n)]
  C --> W
  W --> R[Amortised O(1)]
pitfalls: Quoting big-O without constants when comparing two O(n) approaches.
Forgetting that deleting from the middle of an array is O(n).
Assuming string concatenation in a loop is free — it is often O(n²) overall.

scenario.q: You need 10⁶ lookups by integer key where keys are dense 0…10⁶. Which structure is best?
scenario.why: Dense integer keys let you index directly: O(1) with no hashing, no pointers, and perfect cache locality.

layers.title: Linked Lists, Stacks & Queues
objectives: Implement singly and doubly linked lists safely
Apply LIFO and FIFO disciplines to real problems
Recognise when a pointer structure beats an array
Detect a cycle with Floyd's algorithm

concepts.definition: A record holding a value plus one or more references to other nodes. The structure lives in the links, not in contiguous memory.
A collection where the most recently pushed element is the first popped. Used for call frames, undo history, and depth-first traversal.
A collection where the earliest enqueued element is dequeued first. Used for scheduling, buffering, and breadth-first traversal.
Move one pointer one step and another two steps; if they meet, a cycle exists. O(n) time, O(1) extra space.

layers.intuition: Arrays optimise for random access; linked structures optimise for splicing. If your workload is "insert and delete at known positions", pointers win. If it is "scan and index", arrays win. A stack is a discipline, not a data structure — you can build one on an array or a list, and the constraint is what makes reasoning about it easy.

worked.problem: Reverse a singly linked list in place.
steps: Keep three pointers: prev = null, curr = head, next = null.
While curr exists: save next = curr.next.
Point curr.next = prev (reverse the link).
Advance prev = curr, curr = next.
When the loop ends, prev is the new head.
worked.answer: One pass, O(n) time, O(1) space, original links fully reversed

Forgetting to update tail when the list becomes empty.
Using a linked list where cache-friendly iteration dominates — arrays usually win.

scenario.q: A browser needs "back" navigation with unlimited history. Which structure is the natural fit?
scenario.why: Back navigation is last-in-first-out: the most recently visited page is the first one you return to.

layers.title: Hash Tables & Trees
objectives: Explain hashing, load factor, and collision resolution
Compare chaining with open addressing
Insert, search, and delete in a binary search tree
Choose an ordered structure when range queries matter

concepts.definition: A deterministic map from keys to buckets that spreads keys uniformly. A good hash is fast, stable within a run, and avalanche-sensitive.
Entries divided by buckets. As it approaches 1, collisions and probe lengths explode, so tables resize (usually doubling) around 0.7.
A tree where every left descendant is smaller and every right descendant larger than the node. Search, insert, and delete are O(h) for height h — O(log n) only when balanced.
In-order (left, node, right) yields sorted output for a BST; pre-order and post-order suit serialisation and deletion respectively.

layers.intuition: Hashing trades order for speed: find a key in roughly one step, but lose any notion of "next". Trees keep order at the cost of a logarithmic walk. That trade-off decides architecture: a session cache is a hash table, a range query over timestamps is a tree. Never assume a BST is balanced — a sorted insertion order degenerates it into a linked list.

worked.problem: Insert 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80 into an empty BST, then list an in-order traversal.
steps: 50 becomes the root.
30 < 50 goes left; 70 > 50 goes right.
In-order traversal visits left subtree, node, right subtree at every level.
Result is fully sorted because of the BST invariant.
worked.answer: In-order: 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80 — a perfectly balanced tree of height 3

layers.diagram:
flowchart TD
  K[Key] --> H[hash(key) % buckets]
  H --> B[Bucket index]
  B --> C{Collision?}
  C -->|No| S[Store entry]
  C -->|Yes| R[Chain or probe]
  R --> L{Load factor > 0.7?}
  L -->|Yes| G[Resize and rehash]
  L -->|No| S
pitfalls: Using a mutable object as a key and then mutating it, making the entry unreachable.
Assuming O(1) hash lookups without controlling hash quality and load factor.
Deleting from a BST by simply replacing the node, orphaning subtrees.

scenario.q: You need to fetch the 20 most recent events for a user by timestamp. What fits best?
options: A balanced BST keyed by timestamp, or an index ordered by time
A hash table keyed by event id
A min-heap keyed by random id
scenario.why: The query is a range/order query, which needs an ordered structure; hashing destroys the ordering.

layers.title: Heaps, Tries & Graphs
objectives: Maintain heap order for priority queues
Use a trie for prefix queries
Represent graphs with adjacency lists and matrices
Traverse graphs with BFS and DFS and explain when each is right

concepts.definition: In a min-heap every parent is ≤ its children, so the minimum is at the root. Push and pop are O(log n); building from an array is O(n).
A tree of characters where each path from the root spells a prefix. Lookup costs O(key length), independent of how many keys are stored.
An array of neighbours per vertex, using O(V + E) space. Preferred for sparse graphs; adjacency matrices cost O(V²) but answer edge queries in O(1).
Breadth-first explores level by level and finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs; depth-first dives along one branch and is natural for cycle detection, topological ordering, and backtracking.

layers.intuition: Each structure encodes one question. A heap answers "what is most urgent?" without sorting everything. A trie answers "what starts with this prefix?" without scanning keys. A graph representation answers "who is adjacent?" and the traversal order then determines whether you learn distances (BFS) or structure and reachability (DFS).

worked.problem: Insert 5, 3, 8, 1 into a min-heap (array representation) and show the array after each insertion.
steps: Insert 5 → [5].
Insert 3 → [5, 3], sift up: parent 5 > 3, swap → [3, 5].
Insert 8 → [3, 5, 8], parent 5 < 8 so stop.
Insert 1 → [3, 5, 8, 1], parent at index 1 is 5 > 1, swap → [3, 1, 8, 5].
New parent at index 0 is 3 > 1, swap → [1, 3, 8, 5].
Root is now the minimum and every parent ≤ children.
worked.answer: [1, 3, 8, 5] with the minimum at index 0

pitfalls: Using a heap when you need full sorted order — a heap only guarantees the root.
Storing a trie with per-node hash maps when a dense alphabet array would be faster.
Running BFS with a stack (that is DFS) and then expecting shortest paths.

scenario.q: A task scheduler must always run the highest-priority task next, with tasks arriving continuously. What do you use?
scenario.why: A heap gives O(log n) insertion and O(log n) extraction of the maximum, which is exactly the required access pattern.

layers.title: Advanced Structures & Trade-offs
objectives: Apply union-find with path compression and union by rank
Answer range queries with a segment tree
Explain why balanced trees guarantee logarithmic height
Reason about persistence, concurrency, and cache behaviour

concepts.definition: Tracks disjoint sets with find and union. With path compression and union by rank, operations run in near-constant amortised time, O(α(n)).
A tree over array ranges storing an aggregate per node. Point updates and range queries are O(log n); it is the standard tool for range sums, minima, and maxima.
A BST that rebalances after each mutation to keep height O(log n). Red-black trees allow looser balance for fewer rotations, which is why standard libraries prefer them.
A structure where updates return a new version sharing most nodes with the old one, enabling time-travel queries and cheap snapshots.

layers.intuition: At the frontier, data-structure engineering is about amortising and sharing. Union-find flattens paths so future finds are cheaper; segment trees trade O(n) extra memory for logarithmic range answers; persistence trades pointer indirection for immutable history. The right answer usually follows from the exact mix of reads, writes, and queries — there is no universally best structure.

worked.problem: Build a segment tree over [2, 4, 6, 8] for range sums and query the sum over indices 1…2.
steps: Leaves hold 2, 4, 6, 8.
First level combines pairs: [2+4=6] and [6+8=14].
Root holds 6 + 14 = 20.
Query indices 1…2 straddles both halves: index 1 belongs to the left child, index 2 to the right child.
Descend both sides, read leaf 4 and leaf 6, and combine them: 4 + 6 = 10.
Only O(log n) nodes are visited, and the parent sums are reused for wider ranges.
worked.answer: 10 in O(log n) by visiting only the covering nodes

layers.diagram:
flowchart LR
  Q[Query workload] --> R{Range aggregate?}
  R -->|Yes| S[Segment / Fenwick tree]
  R -->|No| C[Connectivity?]
  C -->|Yes| U[Union-find]
  C -->|No| O[Ordered map]
  O --> B[Balanced BST / B-tree]
pitfalls: Using union-find without path compression and then wondering why finds degrade.
Forgetting that a segment tree needs a merge operation that is associative.
Choosing a persistent structure for a write-heavy workload and paying allocation costs.

scenario.q: You process 10⁶ edges in a graph and repeatedly ask whether two nodes are connected. Best structure?
options: Adjacency matrix plus DFS per query
scenario.why: Dynamic connectivity is exactly the union-find problem; near-constant amortised operations beat repeated traversals.

courses.title: Algorithms
courses.summary: Correctness proofs, sorting, dynamic programming, graph algorithms, and the limits of tractability.

layers.title: Correctness & Growth
objectives: State a loop invariant and use it to prove correctness
Compare functions with asymptotic notation
Set up a recurrence for a recursive algorithm
Distinguish upper bounds from tight bounds

concepts.definition: A property true before and after every iteration. Initialisation, maintenance, and termination together prove the loop computes the intended result.
An equation defining a function in terms of smaller inputs, e.g. T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n for merge sort.
f = Θ(g) when f is both O(g) and Ω(g): the growth rates match up to constants. Big-O alone only promises "no worse than".
Solves T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n) by comparing f(n) with n^(log_b a): the larger term dominates, with a logarithmic factor when they tie.

layers.intuition: An algorithm is a claim plus a proof. The claim is "this returns the right answer in this much time"; the proof is an invariant or a recurrence. Complexity notation is deliberately coarse because constants depend on hardware while growth decides whether the program survives a 100× larger input.

worked.problem: Prove that binary search finds a target in a sorted array.
steps: Invariant: if the target exists, it lies within [lo, hi].
Initialisation: lo = 0, hi = n − 1 covers the whole array, so the invariant holds.
Maintenance: compare with the midpoint; discarding the half that cannot contain the target preserves the invariant.
Termination: each step halves the range, so it becomes empty after ⌈log₂ n⌉ steps.
If the range is empty and nothing matched, the target was never present — the invariant guarantees that conclusion.
worked.answer: Correct by invariant; Θ(log n) comparisons

table.caption: Growth rates you will meet constantly

n = 10⁶ feasibility

layers.diagram:
flowchart LR
  C[Claim] --> I[Invariant or recurrence]
  I --> B[Base case]
  B --> S[Inductive step]
  S --> T[Termination]
  T --> R[Complexity bound]
pitfalls: Confusing O with Θ and calling a loose upper bound tight.
Writing an invariant that is not actually preserved by the loop body.
Ignoring the base case in a recursive proof.

scenario.q: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n. What is the tight bound?
scenario.why: a = 2, b = 2 gives n^(log₂2) = n, which matches f(n) = n, so the master theorem contributes an extra log factor: Θ(n log n).

layers.title: Sorting & Searching
objectives: Trace merge sort and quicksort on a small array
Explain why comparison sorting is Ω(n log n)
Implement binary search over the answer space
Choose a stable sort when order of equals matters

concepts.definition: A sort is stable when equal keys keep their original relative order. Essential when sorting by one field after another.
Split the problem, solve the parts recursively, then combine. Merge sort splits by position; quicksort splits by pivot value.
Quicksort's core step: rearrange so elements left of the pivot are smaller and those right are larger, in linear time and in place.
When a predicate is monotone in a numeric answer, binary search the value range even without an array — e.g. the minimum ship capacity to deliver in D days.

layers.intuition: Sorting is the canonical divide-and-conquer exercise, but the real lesson is about information: each comparison yields one bit, and n! orderings need log₂(n!) ≈ n log n bits, so no comparison sort can beat that. Binary search is the same idea applied to a monotone predicate rather than a list.

worked.problem: Trace merge sort on [5, 2, 9, 1].
steps: Split into [5, 2] and [9, 1].
Split again into [5], [2], [9], [1].
Merge [2, 5] and [1, 9]: take 1, then 2, then 5, then 9 → [1, 2, 5, 9].
worked.answer: [1, 2, 5, 9] with log₂4 = 2 levels of merges

pitfalls: Assuming quicksort is always faster — on adversarial or sorted input with a bad pivot it degrades.
Using an unstable sort for multi-key ordering.
Writing binary search with an off-by-one that skips the last element.

scenario.q: You must sort 10⁷ customer records by last name, then by first name. Which is correct?
options: Sort by first name, then stably by last name
Sort by last name, then unstably by first name
scenario.why: Sorting by the secondary key first and then stably by the primary key preserves the secondary order within equal primary keys.

layers.title: Greedy & Dynamic Programming
objectives: Identify optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems
Prove a greedy choice is safe or find a counterexample
Choose between memoisation and tabulation
Reconstruct a solution from a DP table

concepts.definition: A locally best choice can be part of some global optimum. Interval scheduling has it; 0/1 knapsack does not.
An optimal solution contains optimal solutions to subproblems, which is what makes recursion on subproblems valid.
Top-down recursion that caches results per state. Easy to write from the recurrence; risks stack depth.
Bottom-up filling of a table in dependency order. No recursion overhead and allows space optimisation to the last row.

layers.intuition: Greedy says "commit now and never look back" — fast, but only valid if you can prove exchange arguments. DP says "consider every state once and remember" — slower but robust. Recognise DP when the same subproblem appears in multiple branches; that overlap is what makes caching worth it.

worked.problem: Find the longest common subsequence of "ABCBDAB" and "BDCABA".
steps: Define dp[i][j] = LCS length of the first i and first j characters.
If characters match: dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1] + 1.
Otherwise: dp[i][j] = max(dp[i−1][j], dp[i][j−1]).
Fill row by row; the bottom-right cell gives the length.
Backtrack from the bottom-right, moving diagonally on matches, to recover the string.
worked.answer: LCS length 4, for example "BCBA"
